name: Huperzine A

lead: Huperzine A is an alkaloid from Chinese club moss. In height-maxxing circles it is used for the added-height payoff people want from higher growth hormone, often alongside growth-hormone-boosting routines.

The theory is that blocking acetylcholinesterase lowers somatostatin, the brake on growth hormone, so more is released. Clinical research has studied it for Alzheimer's disease and cognition, not height, and some forum users dispute the somatostatin link.

paras: People take it as an oral supplement, usually as one piece of a wider height or sleep-and-recovery stack, and often alongside growth-hormone-boosting habits. It is also sold as a nootropic. Users who try it for height typically run it over weeks to months and judge results by how they feel and by growth-plate status rather than any measured outcome.

Reported side effects include mild nausea, dizziness and insomnia. It can interact with other cholinesterase inhibitors and anticholinergic drugs. It is a prescription drug for Alzheimer's in China and sold as a supplement in the US. Growth plates close after puberty, so height gains are not expected in adults.

angle.text: Huperzine A is a club-moss extract that height-maxxers take hoping to lower somatostatin, raise growth hormone and gain height. It is approved for Alzheimer's in China and sold as a nootropic; its research is in cognition, and forum users disagree about the height theory.

lead: Huperzine A is a plant alkaloid first isolated in 1983 from the Chinese club moss Huperzia serrata, and a potent, reversible inhibitor of the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, which breaks down the neurotransmitter acetylcholine [1][2][3]. Grokipedia states it has been approved as a prescription drug for Alzheimer's disease in China since 1996 and is sold elsewhere as a dietary supplement marketed for memory and concentration [1][3].

In looksmaxxing communities it appears almost entirely in height-maxxing, where some guides pair it with growth-hormone secretagogues on the theory that raising acetylcholine lowers somatostatin, the hormone that restrains growth hormone release, and so lifts growth hormone [4][5][6]. The chain from this theory to appearance is therefore long: acetylcholine, somatostatin, growth hormone, then growth in height for those whose growth plates are still open. Other forum users dispute the theory, saying they found no study linking huperzine A to somatostatin or height and suggesting the idea came from confusion with a different cholinesterase inhibitor, pyridostigmine [5].

No published human trial has tested huperzine A for height or any other appearance outcome. Clinical research has concentrated on Alzheimer's disease, vascular dementia and cognition [7][8][9][10][11].

paras: The appearance use is height-maxxing. Forum guides describe huperzine A as an adjunct to growth-hormone-raising compounds in the hope of extending height gain during or after puberty, and one looksmax.org thread documents a teenager planning a multi-month programme that pairs a growth-hormone secretagogue with huperzine A [4]. The proposed link is indirect: huperzine A raises acetylcholine by blocking its breakdown, somatostatin-releasing cells are thought by proponents to be inhibited by cholinergic signalling, and lower somatostatin tone would allow more growth hormone release [5]. Somatostatin itself is described as inhibiting growth hormone release from the pituitary, opposing growth-hormone-releasing hormone [6].

Outside appearance circles huperzine A is sold as a nootropic, often in memory-support and pre-workout formulas, and is marketed for memory and concentration [3][12]. Wikipedia also notes use as an oneirogen, a substance taken to influence dreams, likely through cholinesterase inhibition [3]. In China it is a prescription drug for Alzheimer's disease, per Grokipedia [1].

Huperzia serrata, known in Chinese medicine as qian ceng ta, is native to eastern Asia including China, Japan and Korea [13]. Grokipedia describes use of the whole plant for over 1,000 years for bruises, swelling and rheumatism, with records dating to a Tang Dynasty text of 739 AD [1]. Huperzine A was first isolated from the plant in 1983, and a 1989 study found that selagine, an alkaloid described in 1960, was identical to it [3].

A 2004 pharmaceutical profile describes huperzine A as a putative nootropic agent developed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, then in phase III trials in China for Alzheimer's disease, with US and European marketing rights passing in 2003 to a company that planned US trials in age-associated memory loss [14]. The crystal structure of acetylcholinesterase bound to huperzine A was published in 1997 [15].

Huperzine A belongs to the Lycopodium alkaloids, a group of more than 200 alkaloids from club mosses, several of which inhibit acetylcholinesterase [16]. Grokipedia describes the traditional use of Huperzia serrata in Chinese medicine for bruises, swelling and rheumatism, and notes that the plant is slow-growing and wild harvesting raises sustainability concerns [1].

A 2006 review described huperzine A as a highly specific, reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor with better blood-brain barrier penetration, higher oral bioavailability and longer action than tacrine, donepezil and rivastigmine, and with protective effects on cells in animal models [2]. The crystal structure of acetylcholinesterase bound to huperzine A was published in 1997 [15]. A 2017 review discusses it among traditional Chinese medicine ingredients studied for anti-ageing effects [17].
No studies were found testing huperzine A for height, growth hormone or appearance. Research on the compound covers cognition and neurological disease.

Alzheimer's disease: an early Chinese multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial randomised 50 patients to tablet huperzine A and 53 to placebo for eight weeks and assessed memory, dementia and daily-living scales [11]. A US phase 2 trial of 150 participants and a Chinese phase 2/3 trial of sustained-release tablets with 390 participants have been registered [7][8]. A 2019 randomised trial examined cognitive impairment and task-switching in Alzheimer's patients [18]. Wikipedia reports that a 2013 meta-analysis judged the studies to be of poor methodological quality, and that later reviews found very low-quality evidence for daily-living benefits and cognitive benefits with publication bias [3]. Grokipedia summarises meta-analyses as reporting improvements in cognition and daily living, with mild side effects [1]. A 2008 review of eight complementary agents used in Alzheimer's concluded that none had shown clear clinical benefit but that huperzine A, ginkgo and curcumin merited further evaluation [19].

Other conditions: a network meta-analysis of 194 randomised trials in vascular dementia ranked huperzine A among the top five drugs for Mini-Mental State Examination and first for activities-of-daily-living scores [10]. A 1999 double-blind matched-pair study gave huperzine A capsules to 34 pairs of middle-school students complaining of poor memory [20]. Registered studies cover schizophrenia with cognitive impairment, traumatic brain injury, cocaine dependence, cognition and perceived effort during exercise, presbycusis and pharmacokinetics in healthy volunteers [9][21][22][23][24][25]. A 2023 review of over-the-counter memory supplements surveyed 103 products and their ingredients and noted that the FDA does not approve dietary supplements' safety, effectiveness or labeling before sale [12].

Wikipedia lists mild cholinergic effects including nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, slight muscle twitching, slurred speech, hypersalivation and sweating, and says use is not recommended in pregnancy or lactation because of insufficient safety data [3]. Grokipedia lists nausea, dizziness and insomnia as common side effects [1]. Additive effects are possible with other acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, other cholinergic agents and drugs that slow heart rate such as beta blockers [3][1]. Toxicology studies reported in Wikipedia found no toxicity at 50 to 100 times the human therapeutic dose [3].

Supplements in the US are not reviewed by the FDA before sale, and manufacturers are responsible for the safety and truthfulness of their claims [12]. The wild plant is slow-growing, and Grokipedia raises sustainability concerns over wild harvesting [1].

A looksmax.org thread documented an 18-year-old's planned multi-month height-maxxing programme combining a growth-hormone secretagogue with huperzine A; another user answered that such threads rarely deliver the promised updates [4]. A second thread argued that the somatostatin-inhibition claim had spread via a popular height-maxxing guide and was a mix-up with pyridostigmine, saying the author could find no study linking huperzine A to somatostatin [5]. One reply proposed a chain through acetylcholine and somatostatin as a slight possibility, with uncertainty [5].

Pyridostigmine, the compound named in that thread, is a prescription acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used for myasthenia gravis and some other conditions; Wikipedia states that it does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so its effects are mostly peripheral, whereas huperzine A crosses it [26][3]. Height-maxxing discussion of growth hormone more broadly centres on secretagogues and puberty timing rather than on huperzine A.

claims.claim: Huperzine A is a somatostatin inhibitor that raises growth hormone and could add height.
The somatostatin claim is a mix-up with pyridostigmine, so huperzine A does nothing for height.

Huperzine A and pyridostigmine are interchangeable somatostatin inhibitors
